lessons.title: Natural flora and the rules for harvesting
lessons.html:
What natural flora is

Natural flora means plants that grow wild in the veld, fynbos, forest or mountains, not planted by people. South Africa has an unusually rich flora, and many wild plants are harvested for income:

  • Fynbos cut flowers and greens – proteas, pincushions, leucadendrons and buchu in the Western Cape.
  • Honeybush – harvested from the wild in parts of the Western and Eastern Cape for tea.
  • Medicinal plants – bark, roots, bulbs and leaves used in traditional medicine.
  • Thatching grass and reeds – for roofs, mats and crafts.
  • Wild fruits and seeds – such as marula fruit.

Why harvesting must be controlled

If too much is taken, or plants are taken the wrong way, wild populations shrink and can disappear. Some medicinal plants, such as wild ginger and pepper-bark trees, have become rare in the wild because of over-harvesting. Losing plants also harms the animals, birds and insects that depend on them, and the future income of the people who harvest.

Permits and the law

  • Many wild plants are protected. Picking or selling them needs a permit from the provincial conservation authority, such as CapeNature in the Western Cape or Ezemvelo KZN Wildlife in KwaZulu-Natal.
  • You also need permission from the landowner.
  • Some species may not be harvested at all.
  • The permit or harvest plan sets which species, where, how much and when. Carry a copy when harvesting and transporting.

Before you go out

  1. Know exactly which species and which areas are allowed.
  2. Learn to identify the plant correctly. Ask your supervisor to show you.
  3. Take the right tools: sharp secateurs or a knife, bags or crates, gloves.
  4. Tell someone where you are going and when you will return. Take water, a hat and a phone.

lessons.title: Harvesting sustainably and handling the product
lessons.html:
Sustainable harvesting methods

Sustainable means harvesting in a way that lets the plants keep growing and reproducing, so there will be a harvest again next season and for many years.

  • Cut, do not pull. Use sharp secateurs or a knife. Pulling tears roots and can kill the plant.
  • Leave enough on each plant. Take only the amount the harvest plan allows, so the plant can regrow.
  • Leave plants to seed. Leave some flowers and mature plants in every area so that seed falls for new plants.
  • Do not harvest very young plants.
  • Rotate areas. Do not harvest the same patch every season; give it time to recover, as the plan says.
  • Bark: never ring-bark a tree. Take only small strips from one side, if this is allowed.
  • Roots and bulbs: only where permitted; dig carefully and leave part of the population.
  • Stay on paths where possible so you do not trample other plants.

Fire and the veld

Never make fires in the veld. Fynbos and grassland burn easily. Report any smoke at once.

Handling the harvest

  1. Cut at the right stage. For cut flowers, the buyer sets the stage of opening and stem length.
  2. Keep stems in the shade. Heat and sun make flowers and greens wilt.
  3. Do not crush or overfill bags and crates.
  4. Remove damaged, diseased or insect-eaten material.
  5. Bring the harvest to the packshed quickly, where it may be put in water or a cold room.
  6. Keep each species and grade separate and labelled.

Records

Write down the date, area, species and amount harvested. These records show that the permit conditions were followed and help the manager plan future harvests.

Key points

  • Many wild plants are protected; harvest only with a permit and the landowner's permission.
  • Identify plants correctly and follow the harvest plan.
  • Cut, do not pull; leave enough on each plant and leave plants to seed.
  • Rotate harvest areas and never ring-bark trees.
  • Keep the harvest cool and separate, and record what you harvested.
